title: Input and Operators Checkpoint
intro: Your programs can now listen to a person, calculate with what they typed, compare values and combine conditions. Twelve rounds, one from every idea in this module. First-try answers earn three stars!

rounds.prompt: Which line reads a whole number typed at the keyboard into `int age`?
rounds.explain: The arrows point the way the value travels: from `cin` into the variable. `cout <<` is for printing, and `cin << age` does not compile.

rounds.prompt: The person types Amara Okafor. What does this print?
rounds.explain: `cin >>` reads one word and stops at the first space. `getline(cin, name);` would keep the whole line.

rounds.prompt: The Name question is skipped and never waits for an answer. What fixes it?
options: Change getline(cin, name) to cin << name
Add cin.ignore(); straight after cin >> age;
rounds.explain: `cin >> age` leaves the Enter key in the queue, so the following `getline` reads up to it and returns empty. `cin.ignore()` throws that one character away.
`%` gives the remainder. 5 goes into 17 three times with 2 left over, so `/` would give 3 and `%` gives 2.

rounds.prompt: How do you check whether an `int n` is even?
rounds.explain: An even number divides by 2 with nothing left over, so its remainder is 0. Odd numbers leave 1.

rounds.prompt: Splitting a total into units. What does this print?
rounds.explain: `/ 60` gives the whole minutes (62) and `% 60` gives the seconds left over (5). Divide for the big unit, take the remainder for the rest.

rounds.prompt: What does score hold at the end?
rounds.explain: 150 divided by 3 is 50, then `++` adds one to give 51. Each shorthand reads the current value, applies the operator and stores the answer back.

rounds.prompt: The ++ is written after the name. What does this print?
rounds.explain: With the `++` after the name, the old value is handed back first and the increment happens after. `++a` would print 6 twice.

rounds.prompt: A person typed `yes`, stored in a `string` called `answer`. Which line correctly checks it?
rounds.explain: In C++, `==` on a `string` compares the letters one by one. A single `=` would overwrite `answer` instead of asking anything.

rounds.prompt: Careful with the range. What does this print?
rounds.code:
int n = 15;
cout << boolalpha << (1 <= n <= 10) << endl;
rounds.explain: C++ works out `1 <= n` first, which is true and counts as 1, then checks `1 <= 10`, which is always true. Write a range as `n >= 1 && n <= 10`.

rounds.prompt: This crashes when the person enters 0 people. Which version cannot crash?
options: It cannot be fixed without an if statement.
rounds.explain: `&&` stops as soon as the left side is false, so putting the guard first means the division is never reached when people is 0. Order matters.

rounds.prompt: Match each operator to what it does.

pairs.right: Add to a variable and store it back
Ask whether two values are equal
True only when both sides are true
True when at least one side is true

rounds.explain: Six operators across the whole module: one arithmetic, two shorthands, one comparison and two logical.
